coach_says: You were already in serious trouble here, and Ne2 is about as good as anything else; the engine's choices only hold on slightly better. Keep an eye on your rook on c1: it sits on the same diagonal as Black's bishop on h6, with only the queen on g5 in between, so whenever that queen moves the rook can be taken. Moving the rook off c1 early (Rc2) would remove that worry.

Good move. Nd5 adds a second attacker to the knight on f6, which is pinned to the queen by your Bg5, so Black cannot hold it comfortably. This is exactly how to use a pin: pile up on the pinned piece.

Your queen was attacked by the g6 pawn and had to move; Qh3 is a perfectly reasonable square, almost as good as Qe2. Your e6 pawn is going to be hard to keep, so focus on developing quickly (knights out, castle) rather than trying to hold it at all costs.

Black's queen check on e3 had to be answered and Rf2 is a fine way to do it; Kh1 or Kh2 were only marginally better. The one move to avoid was Qf2, which runs into Nxh3+, a knight check that wins your queen. You are worse here mostly because of earlier pawn losses, not this move.

Castling queenside is a sensible choice: it gets your king out of the middle and defends the d7 pawn that the rook on g7 is hitting, while your rook on h8 stays active. You are a piece and pawn down from earlier, so the job now is to stay solid and look for chances.

This endgame is very hard to hold whatever you do, and a5 is about as good as the alternatives. Keep your pawns where the enemy bishop cannot attack them easily and use your king and bishop to blockade White's centre pawns.

Your queen was attacked by the rook on f1 and had to move, but Qg6 sends it to the edge where White's knight can come to f4 and chase it again. Qe4 puts it in the centre, stops Nf4 for free, and hits the d4 pawn, which cannot be defended properly because your bishop on b6 pins it to the White king. When your queen has to move, look for the square where it also attacks something.

White has pushed f3 and g4 with the king still on e1 and the kingside full of holes. The best answer to a pawn storm on the wing is to hit back in the centre: c5 opens lines straight towards White's king and attacks d4 before White can finish developing. c6 is solid but slow, and gives White time for e3 and Nge2 to cover everything.
concept: answer a wing attack in the centre

coach_says: Qh4 attacks the rook on f6, but Black's queen on e7 is lined up on the same diagonal behind that rook. Black plays Rxf1+ with check, you must recapture, and then Qxh4 takes your queen. Before putting your queen on a line with the enemy queen, ask what happens if the piece in between moves with check. Rxf6 first, removing the attacker, kept you clearly better.
also: moving with check gains a tempo

coach_says: Your rook on d5 was attacked by the bishop on c4 and your knight on d4 by the c3 pawn. Nc2 counterattacks the a1 rook, but White simply takes your rook first with Bxd5 and then moves the a1 rook, so you lose the exchange. Rc5 saves the rook by attacking the undefended bishop: if Rd1 then Rxc4, and the trades leave you no worse in material.
concept: lost the exchange to a counterattack

coach_says: Count the attackers on e5: Black hits it with the knights on d7 and c6 and the bishop on g7, three times, and you defend it only twice with Nf3 and Bf4. After castling Black wins it with Ndxe5 and a string of trades. Qe2 adds a third defender down the e-file and keeps your extra space; castling can wait a move.

Your king is still in the middle and your rook on f5 is out in front with few safe squares. After Bd7, White opens the centre with dxe5 dxe5 and then g4 hits the rook: f4 is covered by the c1 bishop and other squares drop it to Nxe5 or Bxg5, so you end up giving the rook for a knight. You needed to act first, for example g4 to kick the f3 knight, rather than make a quiet developing move.

Nd7 lets White swap bishop for knight, and the pawn ending that follows is lost even though you are a pawn up: White's king walks to h5, eats h6, and the f and h pawns run while your king is far away on the queenside. Before allowing a trade into a king and pawn ending, count who reaches the key pawns first. Keep the knight (Nb3 or Ne6) to guard the kingside and you should win.
concept: trade into a lost pawn ending
also: king too far from the action

coach_says: Your rook on f1 was attacked by the bishop on a6, and Rxf7 throws it away for one pawn; after Kxf7 you have no follow-up because your queenside pieces are still at home. The simple d3 blocks the bishop's diagonal and opens the way for your c1 bishop, keeping you clearly better. Only sacrifice when you can see what the extra pieces in the attack will be.

Taking on c4 removes the knight that was guarding your back rank. White plays Rd8+, you must block with Bf8, and Bh6 attacks that pinned bishop: Rxf8 is mate and you cannot cover it. With your king on g8 and no escape square, check that a rook check on d8 is answered before grabbing material. Bg4 instead attacks the d1 rook and keeps you better.

Qxb3 simply wins the bishop back: it looks defended by the a2 pawn, but axb3 is illegal because it would open the a-file and put White's own king on a1 in check from your rook on a8. Always check whether a defending pawn is pinned before assuming a piece is protected. Instead Qf3 let the bishop escape and you stayed a piece down.

Your bishop on e4 was attacked twice, by the knight and the rook. Propping it up with d5 lets White swap Nxe4 dxe4, giving up your good bishop and leaving you with loose pawns on c4 and e4. Just retreat Bb7: from there the bishop eyes g2 down the long diagonal and you keep the pressure on White's weak e3 and h5 pawns.
concept: retreat to keep the good bishop

coach_says: White's queen on c7 is deep in your camp with almost no squares. e5 takes away its last escape routes (d6 is now covered by your f8 bishop) and threatens Ne8, which traps it, winning the queen for a knight. Bg4 instead takes the guard off b7, so Qxb7 escapes and hits your a8 rook and c6 knight. When an enemy queen goes pawn-grabbing, check whether you can cut off its retreat.

After 3...exd4 you should take the pawn back with Nxd4, which also puts your knight on a great central square. Ng5 moves the same knight a second time to attack f7, but nothing else supports it, so Black just develops and you are a pawn down with your knight misplaced. In the opening, win back material and develop before starting an attack.

Qxb5 was the trick: if axb5, Rxa8+ wins the undefended rook with check because the a-file opens, and after Qd8 Rxd8+ Kxd8 you come out a pawn up. Nc6 attacks the queen, but Qc5 hits your g5 bishop and your knight ends up stranded on c6. Look for pawns that cannot capture because moving them opens a line onto something valuable.
concept: pawn pinned to the a8 rook
